title: Compute Landscape: Every Compute & Every Axis
subtitle: Serverless vs classic, all-purpose vs jobs, access modes, SQL warehouses — as axes, not a flat list
mantra: First ask WHAT you run, then WHO manages the machines, and only then turn the knobs.
objectives: You can explain compute as a configuration vector and name the axis behind any setting.
You can draw the Workload × Infrastructure matrix and name all 10 compute types.
You can distinguish all-purpose vs jobs lifecycles and Standard vs Dedicated access mode.
You can tell Standard access mode from Standard performance mode and explain serverless performance modes.
You can compare Serverless / Pro / Classic SQL warehouses and know a notebook on a warehouse runs only SQL/Markdown.
You can choose the right compute for a workload with the one decision diagram.
You can debug 'missing field on serverless', 'unpredictable prod job' and 'unsupported language' situations.

sections.title: Compute = a Configuration Vector
sections.hook: Serverless, Classic, All-purpose, Photon… are not 20 rival products — they are settings of ONE thing.

blocks.text: Your code is just text. `spark.table("prod.sales.orders").groupBy("country").sum("amount")` computes nothing until it gets real resources.
Those resources are **CPU, RAM, network, possibly GPU, a Spark driver and Spark executors**. Databricks calls the whole bundle **compute**.

blocks.label: Think first: Serverless, Classic, All-purpose, Jobs, Standard, Dedicated, Single-node, Autoscaling, GPU, Photon… how many *compute types* is that?
blocks.text: Almost none of them are types. Most are **different characteristics of the same compute** — like colour, engine and gearbox are characteristics of one car, not competing cars.

You will meet all these words: Serverless, Classic, All-purpose, Jobs, Pipeline, Standard, Dedicated, Single-node, Multi-node, Fixed-size, Autoscaling, CPU, GPU, Photon, non-Photon, SQL Serverless, SQL Pro, SQL Classic.

blocks.title: One compute, many axes
blocks.text: A single compute can be **Classic + All-purpose + Standard access + Multi-node + Autoscaling + CPU + Photon + DBR 17.3 LTS**. That whole list is ONE compute configuration.

Compute = (
  workload purpose,      e.g. interactive
  infrastructure model,  e.g. classic
  access mode,           e.g. standard
  topology,              e.g. multi-node
  scaling,               e.g. autoscaling
  hardware,              e.g. CPU
  runtime,               e.g. DBR 17.3
  execution engine       e.g. Photon
)
blocks.caption: Think of compute as a vector of 8 axes

blocks.title: Ordering a car
blocks.text: "Diesel", "automatic" and "red" are not three cars. They are three answers to three different questions about ONE car. Same with "classic", "all-purpose" and "Photon".

blocks.title: Flat-list thinking
blocks.text: Reading the compute page as a flat list of 12+ competing products is the root of most confusion. Always ask: *which axis does this word belong to?*

sections.title: Axis 1 & 2: Purpose vs Infrastructure
sections.hook: "What do I want to do?" and "Who manages the machines?" are two completely different questions.

blocks.text: **Axis 1 — workload purpose** answers: *what do I want to do?* There are four basic categories.

head: Workload
What it means
rows: I sit in a notebook and run cells
Code runs automatically / on a schedule
blocks.caption: Axis 1 — purpose

blocks.text: **Axis 2 — infrastructure model** answers: *who manages the machines?* Two options: **Serverless** or **Classic**.

items.title: Serverless
points: Databricks manages machines, instance types, scaling, server-side runtime, infrastructure lifecycle
You do NOT define 1 driver, 8 workers, m5.4xlarge, DBR X, min 2 / max 10

items.title: Classic
points: You (or a compute policy) define much more
VM type, driver, workers, runtime, autoscaling, access mode, Photon, spot instances…
Classic all-purpose, jobs and pipeline compute are resources YOU create and configure
They run in the customer's cloud account/environment

blocks.title: Different axes
blocks.text: Purpose (interactive/job/pipeline/SQL) is a completely different axis from serverless/classic. Every purpose has to be combined with an infrastructure model.

blocks.title: Taxi vs your own car
blocks.text: Serverless = taxi: you give the destination, the company handles the vehicle. Classic = your own car: you choose the model, engine, tyres and you pay for parking while it sits idle.

blocks.label: Think first: a cluster with `m5.4xlarge` workers, 2–10 autoscaling and DBR 17.3 LTS — serverless or classic?
blocks.text: **Classic.** Picking VM types, worker counts and a DBR version are exactly the decisions serverless takes away from you.

sections.title: The Workload × Infrastructure Matrix
sections.hook: The first map to memorise: every workload has a serverless and a classic flavour — with different product names.

blocks.text: **All-purpose does NOT mean non-serverless.** It roughly means: *reusable interactive classic Spark compute* — the thing you attach notebooks to while experimenting.

09:00 Nikos opens notebook
  ↓ attaches notebook to cluster
09:10 run cell
09:30 another cell
10:20 debugging
11:00 another notebook attaches
blocks.caption: All-purpose = a reusable resource that lives across sessions

blocks.text: Is there a *serverless all-purpose*? Conceptually yes (interactive + serverless), but Databricks does not call it that. It is named **Serverless compute for notebooks**.

INTERACTIVE COMPUTE
├── Serverless → Serverless notebook compute
└── Classic    → Classic all-purpose compute

AUTOMATED WORKLOAD
├── Serverless → Serverless Jobs compute
└── Classic    → Classic Jobs compute

LAKEFLOW PIPELINE
├── Serverless → Serverless pipeline compute
└── Classic    → Classic pipeline compute
blocks.caption: Same split, three times

head: Purpose
Serverless
Classic
blocks.caption: THE matrix to memorise: Workload × Infrastructure

blocks.text: Databricks today recommends **serverless** for most new notebook, job and pipeline workloads.

blocks.title: Different axes — but a constrained matrix
blocks.text: There is no UI with "Purpose: ☑ all-purpose" + "Infrastructure: ☑ serverless" that produces a "serverless all-purpose cluster". interactive + classic is *named* classic all-purpose compute; interactive + serverless is *named* serverless notebook compute. Think **constrained matrix**, not a free Cartesian product.

blocks.title: "Serverless is the opposite of all-purpose"
blocks.text: Wrong level. The opposite of serverless is **classic**. All-purpose describes the interactive/reusable *lifecycle* of a classic compute.

sections.title: The Full Compute Family Tree
sections.hook: Ten compute types to master — six Spark/general, four SQL — arranged as a tree, not a flat list.

blocks.text: For data engineering and analytics you need these **Spark/general compute** types:
The official docs split serverless into **notebooks, jobs and pipelines**, while classic covers **all-purpose, jobs and pipeline** resources.

**SQL compute is a separate family** — SQL Warehouses: (7) Serverless SQL Warehouse, (8) Pro SQL Warehouse, (9) Classic SQL Warehouse, and now (10) **Lakehouse Real-Time SQL Warehouse [Beta]** for very low-latency / high-concurrency read workloads.

DATABRICKS COMPUTE
├── General Spark compute
│   ├── Interactive
│   │   ├── Serverless notebook
│   │   └── Classic all-purpose
│   ├── Automated
│   │   ├── Serverless Jobs
│   │   └── Classic Jobs
│   └── Lakeflow pipelines
│       ├── Serverless pipeline
│       └── Classic pipeline
└── SQL Compute
    ├── Serverless SQL Warehouse
    ├── Pro SQL Warehouse
    ├── Classic SQL Warehouse
    └── Lakehouse Real-Time [Beta]
blocks.caption: A far better mental model than a flat list of 10

blocks.text: Other products also run on serverless infrastructure — **model serving, data-quality monitoring, predictive optimization** — but they are managed from separate product surfaces. Don't put them in the same bucket yet.
There is also **AI Runtime** (Preview) for serverless GPU / deep-learning workloads.

blocks.title: What to master first
blocks.text: As a data engineer, master the 9–10 compute types above first. Model serving, AI Runtime etc. come later.

sections.title: All-purpose vs Jobs: Two Lifecycles
sections.hook: All-purpose lives on between your cells; Jobs compute is born with the run and dies with it.

blocks.text: **All-purpose, concretely:** you create `my-dev-cluster` with Runtime 17.3 LTS, 2–8 workers, autoscaling ON, Standard access.

Notebook A ─┐
Notebook B ─┼──► my-dev-cluster
Notebook C ─┘
blocks.caption: Many notebooks share one reusable cluster

blocks.text: The cluster exists independently of any specific job. You run `spark.read.table(...)`, pause 10 minutes, run another command, debug… That is **all-purpose**: a reusable classic resource not created for one automated run.
**Jobs compute:** a job runs Bronze → Silver at 02:00. You don't need a cluster sitting open at 08:00, 12:00, 18:00.
In **Classic Jobs Compute** you define the cluster configuration; in **Serverless Jobs** Databricks manages it.

blocks.title: Job on all-purpose? Technically yes
blocks.text: Many job task types *can* run on a classic all-purpose cluster, but Databricks does NOT recommend it for production — it prefers serverless jobs or classic jobs compute.

my-dev-cluster (all-purpose)
├── Developer A: running a query
├── Developer B: debugging
└── Job C: production ETL
      → all compete for CPU, RAM,
        executors, shuffle bandwidth
blocks.caption: Why production jobs suffer on shared all-purpose

blocks.text: One developer can destroy the **performance predictability** of the production job.

blocks.title: The name is misleading
blocks.text: **All-purpose ≠ "can do / best for all workloads".** It means *generic reusable interactive compute*.

sections.title: Access Mode: Standard vs Dedicated
sections.hook: Who may use this classic compute, and how are users isolated?

blocks.text: **Access mode** is the next axis. It applies mainly to **classic all-purpose and jobs** compute: **Standard** vs **Dedicated**.

Classic cluster (Standard access)
┌────────────────────────┐
│  Nikos workload        │
│  Maria workload        │
│  John workload         │
└────────────────────────┘
many users, workload isolation
blocks.caption: Standard = shared with isolation

blocks.text: **Standard**: many users can use the same compute with workload isolation. Databricks recommends Standard for **most classic workloads**.

**Dedicated**: the compute is assigned to **one user or a specific group** and is not general shared compute. Used when workloads/features need a more direct environment — e.g. some **ML / GPU / R** scenarios.

head: Lifecycle
Standard
Dedicated
blocks.caption: Classic compute matrix — a real second axis

blocks.text: So valid combos include Classic + All-purpose + Standard, Classic + All-purpose + Dedicated, Classic + Jobs + Standard, Classic + Jobs + Dedicated.

blocks.label: Think first: does serverless have the Standard/Dedicated dropdown?
blocks.text: **No, not in the same way.** You don't create a cluster, so you never write `Access mode = Dedicated`, `Workers = 8`. Those are platform-managed choices. E.g. **serverless Jobs uses Standard access-mode semantics** and requires a workload compatible with Standard compute.

blocks.title: Terminology trap: "standard compute"
blocks.text: "Standard compute" does NOT mean normal/basic compute. Today it means **classic compute configured with Standard access mode**. Likewise **"Dedicated compute" = classic compute configured with Dedicated access mode**.

blocks.title: Standard/Dedicated is not universal
blocks.text: SQL warehouses and serverless don't expose this selector. It is a **classic compute** concept.

sections.title: Topology, Scaling & Hardware
sections.hook: Single vs multi-node, fixed vs autoscaling, CPU vs GPU — three more independent knobs.

blocks.text: **Single-node vs Multi-node** is a classic compute setting.

MULTI-NODE                 SINGLE-NODE
      DRIVER              ┌───────────────────┐
        │                 │ DRIVER + executor │
  ┌─────┼─────┐           │ same machine      │
  ▼     ▼     ▼           └───────────────────┘
WORKER WORKER WORKER      no separate worker VMs
distributed Spark
blocks.caption: Topology axis

blocks.text: Single-node is for **small data, non-distributed libraries, certain ML workloads, development** — not large distributed Spark processing.

items.title: Autoscaling
points: Databricks adds/removes workers within YOUR bounds

items.title: Classic autoscaling
points: YOU: min = 2, max = 10, worker type = X
Databricks: chooses a number between 2 and 10

items.title: Serverless
points: Databricks: handles resource selection AND scaling

blocks.title: Autoscaling ≠ serverless
blocks.text: Classic compute can perfectly well autoscale. Autoscaling is a scaling axis, serverless is an infrastructure axis.
**CPU vs GPU:** classic compute can use CPU instances or **GPU instances** (deep learning). GPU classic compute uses the **ML runtime**, and **Photon is not supported on GPU instance types**.

blocks.code: Classic + All-purpose + Dedicated + GPU + DBR ML
blocks.caption: A perfectly sensible configuration

blocks.text: Since 2026 **AI Runtime** (Public Preview) brings **serverless GPU** infrastructure for deep learning. So GPU and serverless are not opposites — again, different axes.

blocks.title: Constraint between axes
blocks.text: GPU + Photon on classic GPU compute ❌. Not every combination of axis values is allowed.

sections.title: Runtime & Photon as Axes
sections.hook: DBR is software, Photon is an execution engine — neither is a compute family.

blocks.text: On classic compute you pick a **Databricks Runtime (DBR)** such as `DBR 17.3 LTS` or a `DBR ML` variant. That is a **software stack**, not hardware.

blocks.code:
AWS VM:  m5.xlarge      <- hardware
software: DBR 17.3 LTS  <- runtime
blocks.caption: Hardware and runtime are separate choices

blocks.text: The runtime includes **Spark plus Databricks software/libraries**.

items.title: Serverless
points: Databricks upgrades the server-side runtime; **serverless environment versions** give application compatibility

blocks.text: **Photon** on classic CPU compute: **ON or OFF** — your choice. On **serverless**: Photon enabled, managed by Databricks. **SQL warehouses** also use Photon.

blocks.title: Photon is an axis, not a family
blocks.text: There is no "Photon compute" product. Photon is a setting (engine) that sits on top of a compute.

blocks.title: "Which DBR for my serverless job?"
blocks.text: Usually the wrong question: on serverless you don't pin a traditional DBR version.

sections.title: The Classic Matrix & What Serverless Removes
sections.hook: Classic = a dozen knobs; serverless = "here is my workload, run it".

blocks.text: **Example 1 — interactive ETL development:** All-purpose · Classic · Standard · DBR 17.3 LTS · Photon ON · Multi-node · general-purpose worker · 2 → 8 workers · general-purpose driver. That is **one classic all-purpose compute with 9 configuration choices**, not 10 computes.
**Example 2 — production scheduled ETL:** Jobs · Classic · Standard · DBR 17.3 LTS · Photon ON · Multi-node · autoscaling 4 → 20 workers → a **Classic Jobs Compute** with specific parameters.

**Serverless equivalent:** Purpose = Jobs, Infrastructure = Serverless. Now you do NOT choose driver VM, worker VM, 2–20 workers, DBR 17.3, spot or pool. **Autoscaling and Photon are enabled automatically** in serverless Jobs.

Order of decisions: first decide *Classic all-purpose* or *Classic Jobs*; **only then** go into Standard/Dedicated, Single/Multi, DBR, CPU/GPU, worker type, driver type, Fixed/Autoscaling, Photon, Spot, Pools, auto termination.

blocks.title: Not supported on serverless
blocks.text: Serverless does NOT support **compute policies, instance pools, compute-scoped init scripts, compute-scoped libraries**, or most **Spark cluster configurations** — these infrastructure concerns are platform-managed.

blocks.title: Classic = 'large matrix', Serverless = 'matrix disappears'
blocks.text: That disappearance is the whole point of serverless.

sections.title: Serverless Performance Modes
sections.hook: Serverless still has a knob — speed vs cost — and its name collides with an access mode.

blocks.text: For serverless **Jobs and Pipelines** there is a **performance mode**: **Performance Optimized** vs **Standard**.

head: Serverless workload
Performance optimized
Standard
blocks.caption: Serverless matrix — notebooks use a performance-oriented interactive mode

blocks.title: Standard access ≠ Standard performance
blocks.text: **Standard access mode** = security/isolation concept for classic compute (who may use it, how users are isolated). **Standard performance mode** = serverless cost/latency concept (lower cost or faster startup?). Nothing in common except the English word.

blocks.label: Think first: a nightly 02:00 batch ETL with no SLA on start time — which serverless performance mode?
blocks.text: **Standard** performance mode: slower startup doesn't matter at 02:00, and it costs less.

sections.title: SQL Warehouses: Serverless, Pro, Classic
sections.hook: The SQL family is its own branch — with its own feature ladder.

blocks.text:
SQL WAREHOUSE
├── Serverless
├── Pro
└── Classic
blocks.caption: A different branch from Spark/general compute

blocks.text: **All** current warehouse types support **Photon**. **Serverless** additionally has **Predictive IO + Intelligent Workload Management**. **Pro** has Photon + Predictive IO. **Classic** has Photon only.

blocks.title: Feature ladder mnemonic
blocks.text: **Classic = P**, **Pro = P + P**, **Serverless = P + P + I**: Photon → + Predictive IO → + Intelligent Workload Management.
Can a **notebook attach to a SQL warehouse**? Yes — but it can only run **SQL and Markdown** cells, not Python/R.

blocks.caption: ✅ SQL cell

blocks.code:
# fails in a notebook attached ONLY to a SQL warehouse
from pyspark.sql import functions as F
blocks.caption: ❌ Python cell

blocks.title: Python on a SQL warehouse
blocks.text: A notebook attached exclusively to a SQL warehouse cannot run Python cells. Attach to serverless notebook compute or all-purpose for PySpark.

blocks.title: Constraints between axes
blocks.text: If you choose serverless, many axes are managed by Databricks (no worker type, no pool…). And on classic GPU compute, GPU + Photon is not possible. The axes are real but **constrained**.

DATABRICKS COMPUTE
                     │
     FIRST QUESTION: What is my workload?
                     │
  ┌────────────┬─────┴──────┬────────────┐
INTERACTIVE   JOB        PIPELINE       SQL
  │            │            │            │
choose infra choose infra choose infra  SQL WH
 ┌─┴─┐        ┌─┴─┐        ┌─┴─┐      ┌──┼───┐
 S   C        S   C        S   C      S Pro  C
     │
 ALL-PURPOSE → configure: Standard/Dedicated,
   Single/Multi, Fixed/Autoscale, CPU/GPU,
   DBR, Photon
S = Serverless   C = Classic
blocks.caption: The ONE diagram to remember

blocks.text: **Example A:** "Explore 500 GB of customer transactions." Step 1: interactive (I'll try commands). Step 2: custom infra? No → **Serverless notebook compute**. Done — no worker VMs to decide.
**Example B:** "Run ETL every night at 2 a.m." automated + no special infra → **Serverless Jobs**.

**Example C:** nightly ETL using a **custom Spark JAR and low-level Spark functionality** not supported on serverless → automated + classic required → **Classic Jobs Compute**, then choose DBR, workers, autoscaling, access mode, Photon…

**Example D:** 100 analysts run SQL from **Power BI**. Not an all-purpose cluster! SQL/BI → SQL Warehouse → usually **Serverless SQL Warehouse** (recommended today for BI, SQL ETL and exploratory analytics).

**Example E:** "I want an **R** notebook." Serverless notebooks don't support **R** (the source also lists Scala and **RDD APIs** as unsupported). Interactive + unsupported serverless feature → **Classic all-purpose**, possibly **Dedicated**.

blocks.title: Ask yourself when choosing compute
questions: Am I sitting and trying commands (interactive), scheduling something (job), building a declarative pipeline, or serving SQL/BI?
Do I need anything serverless doesn't support (R, RDD APIs, custom JAR/low-level Spark, init scripts, pools, specific Spark configs)?
If not — why wouldn't I use serverless?
If classic: have I decided all-purpose vs jobs BEFORE touching the parameters?
Is this SQL/BI? Then why am I looking at Spark clusters instead of a SQL warehouse?

debug.title: My R / RDD notebook fails on serverless
debug.symptom: A notebook using R (or RDD APIs) fails or the language isn't available when attached to serverless notebook compute.
askYourself: Is this notebook running on serverless notebook compute?
Does my code use something serverless notebooks don't support (R, RDD APIs; the source also lists Scala)?
Can I rewrite it with DataFrame/SQL APIs that serverless supports?
If not, do I need classic all-purpose — and does the workload need Dedicated access?

steps.do: Check which compute the notebook is attached to.
steps.why: Serverless notebook compute has language/API limits.
Decides whether a rewrite or a compute change is needed.

steps.do: Attach to a classic all-purpose cluster (Dedicated if required).
steps.why: Interactive + unsupported serverless feature → classic all-purpose.

rootCauses: Serverless notebooks don't support R or RDD APIs.
debug.fix: Use classic all-purpose compute (possibly Dedicated access) for R/RDD development, or rewrite to DataFrame/SQL to stay on serverless.

debug.title: I can't find worker type / pool / init script fields on my serverless job
debug.symptom: You try to set worker type, min/max workers, an instance pool, a compute policy or a compute-scoped init script on serverless Jobs and the fields don't exist.
askYourself: Am I on serverless or classic?
Is the setting I want an infrastructure concern (VMs, counts, pools, init scripts, policies, Spark cluster configs)?
Does my workload truly need that setting, or was I copying a classic habit?
If it truly needs it, should this be Classic Jobs compute?

steps.do: Confirm the job's compute is serverless.
steps.why: Serverless hides the infrastructure envelope by design.

steps.do: Check whether the requirement is real (e.g. custom JAR/low-level Spark).
steps.why: Most workloads don't need these knobs.

steps.do: If required, switch the task to Classic Jobs compute and configure there.
steps.why: Classic exposes VM type, workers, pools, init scripts, policies.

rootCauses: Serverless doesn't support compute policies, instance pools, compute-scoped init scripts, compute-scoped libraries or most Spark cluster configs.
debug.fix: Let serverless manage infrastructure; if a classic-only feature is required, use Classic Jobs compute.
debug.mnemonic: No PIPS on serverless: Policies, Init scripts, Pools, Spark confs.

debug.title: Production job runtime is unpredictable
debug.symptom: A scheduled production ETL takes 20 min some nights and 90 min others; it runs on a shared all-purpose cluster.
askYourself: Which compute does this job run on — all-purpose, classic jobs or serverless jobs?
Who else is attached to that cluster at the same time?
Are developers' notebooks competing for CPU, RAM, executors, shuffle bandwidth?
Is this one of the limited exceptions (iterative job testing, very short frequent jobs) — or real production?
Can I move it to serverless Jobs or classic Jobs compute?

steps.do: Look at the job's compute setting.
steps.why: All-purpose is shared and interactive by design.

steps.do: Check other activity on that cluster during the run.
Switch the job to serverless Jobs (or classic Jobs compute).
steps.why: Jobs compute's lifecycle is tied to the run — isolated and predictable.

rootCauses: Resource contention on shared all-purpose compute.
Using all-purpose for production against Databricks' recommendation.
debug.fix: Run production jobs on serverless Jobs or classic Jobs compute.

debug.title: Python cell fails in a notebook attached to a SQL warehouse
debug.symptom: SQL cells run fine, but `from pyspark.sql import functions as F` fails in the same notebook.
askYourself: What is this notebook attached to — a SQL warehouse or Spark compute?
Which cell languages does a SQL warehouse run (SQL + Markdown only)?
Can this logic be expressed in SQL instead?
If I need Python, should I attach serverless notebook compute or all-purpose?

steps.do: Check the attached compute in the notebook header.
steps.why: Warehouses only run SQL and Markdown.

steps.do: Rewrite in SQL or re-attach to Spark compute.

rootCauses: Notebook attached exclusively to a SQL warehouse.
debug.fix: Attach the notebook to serverless notebook compute (or classic all-purpose) for Python, or keep SQL-only cells on the warehouse.

debug.title: Serverless job/pipeline starts too slowly (or costs more than expected)
debug.symptom: A serverless job or pipeline has slow startup that breaks an SLA — or a batch job is more expensive than needed.
askYourself: Is this a serverless Job/pipeline or a notebook (notebooks have no Standard performance mode)?
Which performance mode is set: Standard or Performance Optimized?
Does this workload need fast startup (latency-sensitive) or is it batch with slack?
Am I confusing performance mode with Standard ACCESS mode?

steps.do: Open the job/pipeline settings and read the performance mode.
Latency-sensitive → Performance Optimized; batch with slack → Standard.

rootCauses: Standard performance mode on a latency-sensitive workload.
Performance Optimized on a relaxed batch workload (paying for speed you don't need).
debug.fix: Match the performance mode to the SLA: Performance Optimized for fast startup, Standard for cheaper batch.
debug.mnemonic: Fast or cheap — pick the mode.

debug.title: Photon option unavailable on my GPU cluster
debug.symptom: On a classic GPU cluster with DBR ML, Photon can't be enabled.
askYourself: Is this classic compute on GPU instance types?
Do I actually need Photon (SQL/DataFrame engine) or the GPU (deep learning)?
Should SQL/ETL parts run on a separate CPU compute with Photon?

steps.do: Confirm the instance type is GPU.
steps.why: Photon isn't supported on GPU instance types.

steps.do: Split workloads: GPU compute for DL, CPU + Photon for ETL.

rootCauses: Axis constraint: GPU + Photon is not allowed on classic GPU compute.
debug.fix: Accept no Photon on GPU compute, or run SQL/ETL on CPU compute with Photon.

debug.title: Workload fails on serverless Jobs but worked on my Dedicated cluster
debug.symptom: Code that ran on a classic Dedicated cluster fails after moving the task to serverless Jobs.
askYourself: Does serverless Jobs use Standard access-mode semantics?
Was my code relying on something only Dedicated (single-user/direct) environments allow?
Is the failing feature in the serverless-unsupported list (R, RDD, init scripts, Spark configs)?
Should this task stay on classic Jobs compute with Dedicated access?

steps.do: Read the error and identify the feature used.
Refactor to Standard-compatible APIs, or keep classic Jobs + Dedicated.

rootCauses: Serverless Jobs = Standard access semantics; Dedicated-only features fail.
debug.fix: Make the workload Standard-compatible or run it on classic Jobs compute with Dedicated access.

pitfalls.title: Serverless is the opposite of all-purpose
pitfalls.text: They live on different axes: serverless/classic is infrastructure, all-purpose/jobs is lifecycle/purpose.
pitfalls.fix: Opposite of serverless = classic. Classic interactive = all-purpose.

pitfalls.title: Looking for a 'serverless all-purpose cluster'
pitfalls.text: Interactive + serverless is named serverless notebook compute; the matrix is constrained.
pitfalls.fix: Use the Workload × Infrastructure matrix names.

pitfalls.title: All-purpose = best for everything
pitfalls.text: The name is misleading: it means generic reusable interactive compute.
pitfalls.fix: Use Jobs compute (serverless or classic) for production jobs.

pitfalls.title: Production jobs on shared all-purpose
pitfalls.text: Developers compete with the job for CPU, RAM, executors, shuffle bandwidth — no predictability.
pitfalls.fix: Serverless Jobs or classic Jobs compute.

pitfalls.title: Autoscaling = serverless
pitfalls.text: Classic compute autoscales between min and max that YOU set.
pitfalls.fix: Autoscaling is a scaling axis; serverless is an infrastructure axis.

pitfalls.title: Standard access vs Standard performance
pitfalls.text: Same word, unrelated concepts: security/isolation vs serverless cost/startup.
pitfalls.fix: Ask: classic security question or serverless speed/cost question?

pitfalls.title: 'Standard compute' = basic compute
pitfalls.text: It means classic compute with Standard access mode.

pitfalls.title: Expecting a Standard/Dedicated dropdown on serverless
pitfalls.text: Serverless hides it; serverless Jobs uses Standard semantics.

pitfalls.title: Setting worker type / min-max / pools on serverless
pitfalls.text: Serverless manages infrastructure and doesn't support pools, policies, compute-scoped init scripts/libraries, most Spark configs.
pitfalls.fix: Let it go, or use classic if truly required.

pitfalls.title: Photon on GPU classic compute
pitfalls.text: Photon isn't supported on GPU instance types.
pitfalls.fix: GPU for DL; CPU + Photon for ETL/SQL.

pitfalls.title: Python cells on a SQL warehouse
pitfalls.text: Notebooks on a SQL warehouse run only SQL and Markdown.
pitfalls.fix: Attach to serverless notebook or all-purpose for Python.

pitfalls.title: R on serverless notebooks
pitfalls.text: Serverless notebooks don't support R (nor RDD APIs).

pitfalls.title: Standard performance mode for notebooks
pitfalls.text: Notebooks only use the performance-oriented interactive mode.
pitfalls.fix: Standard performance mode is for serverless Jobs/pipelines.

pitfalls.title: All-purpose cluster for BI
pitfalls.text: Power BI / dashboards are a SQL/BI workload.

pitfalls.title: Pinning a DBR on serverless
pitfalls.text: Serverless manages the server runtime; you choose environment versions instead.

flashcards.a: The resources used to execute a workload: CPU, RAM, network, possibly GPU, Spark driver and executors.

flashcards.q: Name the 8 axes of the compute configuration vector.
flashcards.a: Purpose, infrastructure, access mode, topology, scaling, hardware, runtime, execution engine.
Interactive, Job, Pipeline, SQL.
Serverless vs Classic — who manages the machines.
In the customer's cloud account/environment.
Serverless compute for notebooks (serverless notebook compute).
Classic all-purpose compute.
Classic (not all-purpose).
Axes are conceptually independent, but only certain named products exist (no 'serverless all-purpose').
Serverless notebook, classic all-purpose, serverless Jobs, classic Jobs, serverless pipeline, classic pipeline.
Serverless, Pro, Classic, Lakehouse Real-Time [Beta].

flashcards.q: Lakehouse Real-Time SQL Warehouse is for…
flashcards.a: Very low-latency / high-concurrency read workloads (Beta).
Serverless GPU infrastructure for deep learning (Preview).
Job start → compute starts → run → job ends → compute goes away.

flashcards.q: Can a job run on all-purpose?
flashcards.a: Technically yes for many task types, but not recommended for production.
Many users share classic compute with workload isolation; recommended for most classic workloads.
Compute assigned to one user or group; for some ML/GPU/R scenarios.
Classic compute configured with Standard access mode.
Standard access-mode semantics; workload must be Standard-compatible.
Small data, non-distributed libraries, certain ML, development.
Different axes; classic can autoscale within your min/max.
Not supported.
Classic: you choose the DBR. Serverless: Databricks manages the runtime; you get environment versions.
Enabled and managed by Databricks.
Compute policies, instance pools, compute-scoped init scripts, compute-scoped libraries (and most Spark cluster configs).
Autoscaling and Photon.
Performance Optimized (fast startup) vs Standard (slower startup, lower cost, batch).

flashcards.q: Which serverless workload lacks Standard performance mode?
flashcards.a: Notebooks.
Security/isolation (classic) vs cost/startup trade-off (serverless). Unrelated.
Classic: Photon. Pro: + Predictive IO. Serverless: + Intelligent Workload Management.

flashcards.q: Notebook on a SQL warehouse can run…
flashcards.a: SQL and Markdown only.
Serverless SQL Warehouse.
Classic Jobs.
Serverless SQL Warehouse (alt: Pro).

flashcards.q: First question in the decision diagram?
flashcards.a: What is my workload?

exercises.q: Which list best describes what **compute** means in Databricks?
options: CPU, RAM, network, possibly GPU, a Spark driver and Spark executors used to run the workload
The Delta tables your query reads
why: Code needs compute to run; it isn't compute.
Correct — the bundle of execution resources.
Tables are data, stored outside compute.
The metastore holds metadata, not execution resources.
exercises.explain: Compute is the set of real resources Databricks uses to execute a workload. Code alone is just text and does no computation; tables and metastores are data/metadata, not the execution resources.

exercises.q: Serverless, Classic, All-purpose, Jobs, Standard, Dedicated, Photon and GPU are twelve-ish competing compute types you pick one of.
exercises.explain: Most of these words are **characteristics (axes) of the same compute**. One compute can be Classic + All-purpose + Standard + Multi-node + Autoscaling + CPU + Photon + DBR 17.3 LTS at the same time.

exercises.q: Match each value to the axis it belongs to.
exercises.explain: This is the configuration vector: purpose, infrastructure, access, topology, scaling, hardware, runtime, engine. Each word answers a different question about the SAME compute.

exercises.q: Complete the configuration vector.
exercises.text: Compute = (workload [[purpose]], [[infrastructure]] model, [[access]] mode, topology, [[scaling]], hardware, [[runtime]], execution [[engine]])
exercises.explain: The eight axes: purpose, infrastructure, access mode, topology, scaling, hardware, runtime, execution engine. Learning which axis each UI option belongs to removes most confusion.

exercises.q: In your own words: why is it wrong to think of the Databricks compute page as a flat list of compute types?
exercises.model: Because most terms are values on different axes of one compute configuration. Serverless/classic is about who manages infrastructure, all-purpose/jobs about lifecycle/purpose, Standard/Dedicated about access, Photon about the execution engine, DBR about software. One compute combines one value from each axis, so 'Classic + All-purpose + Standard + Photon' is one compute, not four.
rubric: Most terms are axes/characteristics, not types
One compute = one value per axis (configuration vector)
exercises.explain: A flat list hides that the words answer different questions. Thinking in axes lets you read any configuration as a vector of choices.

exercises.q: Which one is NOT a characteristic/axis value of a single compute configuration?
exercises.explain: `prod.sales.orders` is a table (data), not a compute setting. Autoscaling (scaling), Photon (engine) and Standard (access mode) are all axis values of one compute.

exercises.q: Sort: which axis does each phrase answer?
buckets: Axis 1: What do I want to do?
exercises.explain: Purpose (interactive / job / pipeline / SQL) is one axis; infrastructure model (serverless / classic) is a completely different axis.

exercises.q: On **serverless** compute, which of these do you still decide yourself?
why: Instance types are managed by Databricks.
Server-side runtime is managed by Databricks.
exercises.explain: With serverless you say 'run the workload' and Databricks manages machines, instance types, scaling, server-side runtime and lifecycle. VM types, worker counts and DBR pinning are classic decisions.

exercises.q: Classic all-purpose, jobs and pipeline compute run in the customer's cloud account/environment and are resources you create and configure.
exercises.explain: That is the classic model: you (or a compute policy) define VM type, driver, workers, runtime, autoscaling, access mode, Photon, spot instances, etc., and the VMs live in your cloud account.

exercises.q: Who decides it? Sort each item.
exercises.explain: In classic you configure the infrastructure envelope; in serverless the infrastructure (machines, instance types, scaling, runtime server side, lifecycle) is Databricks-managed.

exercises.q: Explain serverless vs classic with an everyday analogy.
exercises.model: Serverless is like a taxi: you give the destination (your workload) and the company handles the vehicle, maintenance and scaling. Classic is like owning a car: you choose the model (VM type), how many (workers), the engine (runtime/Photon), and you pay while it sits idle.
rubric: Serverless: you specify the workload only
Mentions who manages lifecycle/cost of idle
exercises.explain: Any analogy works if it separates 'what I want done' from 'who owns and configures the machines'.

exercises.q: What is the **classic** equivalent of **serverless notebook compute**?
exercises.explain: Interactive + serverless = serverless notebook compute; interactive + classic = classic all-purpose compute. Jobs compute is for automated runs, warehouses for SQL.

exercises.q: What is the classic equivalent of **serverless Jobs compute**?
exercises.explain: Automated workload: serverless → Serverless Jobs compute, classic → Classic Jobs compute. All-purpose is the interactive classic flavour.

exercises.q: Serverless is the opposite of all-purpose.
exercises.explain: Different levels. The infrastructure opposite of serverless is **classic**. All-purpose describes an interactive/reusable classic workload lifecycle.

exercises.q: Complete the Workload × Infrastructure matrix: match each (purpose + infra) to its product name.
exercises.explain: This matrix is the first map to memorise. Notice that the interactive/serverless product is NOT called 'serverless all-purpose'.

exercises.q: In the UI you can tick 'Purpose: all-purpose' and 'Infrastructure: serverless' to create a serverless all-purpose cluster.
exercises.explain: There is no such pair of dropdowns. Interactive + serverless is the product **serverless notebook compute**. Purpose and infrastructure are different axes conceptually, but the matrix is constrained, not a free Cartesian product.

exercises.q: Fill in the product names.
exercises.text: INTERACTIVE → Serverless: [[Serverless notebook compute|serverless compute for notebooks|serverless notebook]] / Classic: [[Classic all-purpose compute|all-purpose compute|all-purpose]]
exercises.explain: Databricks names the serverless interactive option 'Serverless compute for notebooks'; the classic one is all-purpose compute.

exercises.q: What does **all-purpose** actually mean?
options: Reusable interactive classic Spark compute you attach notebooks to
A cluster that can run SQL warehouses
why: Classic is the opposite of serverless; all-purpose is a lifecycle.
The name misleads — it's not the best choice for all.
exercises.explain: All-purpose is a lifecycle concept: a reusable classic resource that lives across interactive sessions. It is not a synonym of 'non-serverless' and not 'best for everything'.

exercises.q: How many **Spark/general** compute types (serverless + classic flavours of interactive, automated and pipeline) are in the list?
exercises.explain: Interactive, automated and pipeline × serverless/classic = 3 × 2 = 6: serverless notebook, classic all-purpose, serverless jobs, classic jobs, serverless pipeline, classic pipeline.

exercises.q: How many SQL warehouse types are listed, counting the Beta one?
exercises.explain: Serverless, Pro, Classic, plus Lakehouse Real-Time SQL Warehouse [Beta] for very low-latency/high-concurrency reads = 4. Together with the 6 Spark types that's the 10 compute types to master.

exercises.q: Put each compute type into its family.
exercises.explain: SQL warehouses are a separate family from the six Spark/general compute types.

exercises.q: Which one should NOT be put in the same bucket as the core data-engineering compute types (yet)?
exercises.explain: Model serving (like data-quality monitoring and predictive optimization) uses serverless infrastructure but is managed from a separate product surface. The other three are core compute types.

exercises.q: What is the **Lakehouse Real-Time SQL Warehouse [Beta]** for?
exercises.explain: It is a new SQL warehouse type for particularly low-latency, high-concurrency reads. Serverless GPU deep learning is AI Runtime.

exercises.q: AI Runtime (Preview) provides serverless GPU infrastructure for deep-learning workloads.
exercises.explain: AI Runtime brings serverless GPU — which proves GPU and serverless are not opposite concepts.

exercises.q: Order the **Jobs compute** lifecycle.
exercises.explain: Jobs compute is born with the run and terminates with it — no cluster sitting open at 08:00, 12:00, 18:00 for a 02:00 job.

exercises.q: A job task can never run on a classic all-purpose cluster.
exercises.explain: Technically many job task types can use all-purpose compute. Databricks just doesn't recommend it for production — it prefers serverless jobs or classic jobs compute.

exercises.q: Why does Databricks discourage running production ETL on a shared all-purpose cluster?
options: Developers' queries compete with the job for CPU, RAM, executors and shuffle bandwidth, killing predictability
Jobs can't be scheduled on all-purpose
exercises.explain: Shared resources mean a developer's heavy query can destroy the performance predictability of the production job. All-purpose can read Delta and can autoscale — those distractors are false.

exercises.q: 'All-purpose' means it is the best choice for all workloads.
exercises.explain: The name is misleading. It means generic reusable interactive compute, not 'optimal for everything'.

exercises.q: All-purpose or Jobs compute?

items.text: Exists independently of any specific job
Pause 10 min, then run another cell

exercises.explain: All-purpose is a reusable interactive resource; Jobs compute's lifecycle is tied to the run.

exercises.q: Your nightly production ETL runs on `my-dev-cluster` (shared all-purpose). Run times vary wildly: 20 minutes some nights, 90 minutes others.

options.text: Resource contention: other users/notebooks share the cluster
options.fb: Yes — on all-purpose, developers and the job compete for CPU, RAM, executors and shuffle bandwidth.

options.text: The Delta table is corrupt
options.fb: Nothing points to corruption; variable runtime on a shared cluster points to contention.

options.text: Photon is broken
options.fb: Photon doesn't cause night-to-night variance tied to other users.

options.text: Move the job to serverless Jobs (or classic Jobs compute)
options.fb: Correct — jobs compute gives the run its own lifecycle and isolated resources.

options.text: Ask developers to stop working at night forever
options.fb: Fragile and doesn't fix billing/idle issues; use the intended compute.

options.text: Make the all-purpose cluster Dedicated to the job
options.fb: That still keeps an always-on interactive cluster; Jobs compute is the operational model.

exercises.explain: All-purpose = interactive by design. Production jobs belong on serverless Jobs or classic Jobs compute for predictable performance.

exercises.q: Which access mode does Databricks recommend for **most classic workloads**?
exercises.explain: Standard: many users share the compute with workload isolation. Dedicated is for one user/group when features need a more direct environment (some ML/GPU/R).

exercises.q: When someone says "standard compute" in today's Databricks terminology, they mean a basic/normal cluster.
exercises.explain: "Standard compute" = classic compute configured with **Standard access mode**. "Dedicated compute" = classic compute configured with Dedicated access mode.

exercises.q: A classic all-purpose compute can be either Standard or Dedicated.
exercises.explain: Yes — Standard/Dedicated are explicit access-mode options for both classic all-purpose and classic jobs compute.

exercises.q: Does **serverless Jobs** have a Standard/Dedicated dropdown?
options: Yes, Standard by default and you can switch
No — the platform manages it; serverless Jobs uses Standard access-mode semantics and needs Standard-compatible workloads
No — serverless has no security at all
why: Serverless has access management, just not this selector.
exercises.explain: In serverless you don't create a cluster or set access mode/workers. Serverless Jobs uses Standard access semantics, so workloads must be compatible with Standard compute.

exercises.q: Match the classic-compute matrix cell to its value.
exercises.explain: Standard/Dedicated is explicit for all-purpose and jobs compute; pipelines have their own configuration model; serverless hides the selector.

exercises.q: Which scenario is the odd one out (doesn't point to Dedicated access)?
options: R development needing a direct environment
A compute assigned to a single data scientist group
20 analysts sharing a cluster with workload isolation
exercises.explain: Many users sharing with isolation is **Standard**. Dedicated is assigned to one user/group and used for some ML/GPU/R scenarios.

exercises.q: Autoscaling means serverless.
exercises.explain: Classic compute can autoscale perfectly well (you set min/max; Databricks picks a number between). Autoscaling ≠ serverless.

exercises.q: A **fixed-size** classic cluster has `workers = 4`. During a heavy spike, how many workers does it have?
exercises.explain: Fixed means fixed: 4 workers all the time. Only autoscaling clusters move between min and max.

exercises.q: An autoscaling classic cluster has min 2, max 10 workers. What is the most workers it can reach under the heaviest load?
exercises.explain: Databricks adds/removes workers but only inside the bounds YOU set: 2–10. It will never go to 11 on its own.

exercises.q: Single-node or multi-node?

items.text: Driver acts as executor on the same machine

exercises.explain: Single-node has no separate worker VMs — fine for small data, dev, non-distributed libraries and some ML, not for large distributed Spark.

exercises.q: This classic compute spec has an invalid combination. Click the bad line.
exercises.fix: Photon: OFF (Photon is not supported on GPU instance types)
exercises.explain: Classic GPU compute uses the ML runtime and Photon is not supported on GPU instance types. Classic + All-purpose + Dedicated + GPU + DBR ML is otherwise a perfectly sensible config.

exercises.q: GPU and serverless are opposite concepts: if you need GPU you must use classic.
exercises.explain: AI Runtime (Public Preview, 2026) brings serverless GPU infrastructure for deep learning. GPU (hardware) and serverless (infrastructure model) are different axes.

exercises.q: Complete the comparison.
exercises.text: Classic autoscaling: YOU set [[min]] = 2 and [[max]] = 10 and the worker type; Databricks chooses a number between them. Serverless: YOU say "run my [[workload]]" and Databricks handles resource selection and [[scaling]].
exercises.explain: The difference is who owns the bounds and resource choice. Classic autoscaling is still you configuring infrastructure.

exercises.q: On classic compute, choosing `DBR 17.3 LTS` selects…
exercises.explain: The runtime is software, not hardware. `m5.xlarge` would be the hardware choice.

exercises.q: On serverless compute you pick a traditional DBR version like `DBR 17.3` from a dropdown.
exercises.explain: Databricks upgrades the server-side runtime itself and uses **serverless environment versions** for application compatibility. 'Classic: I choose the DBR; serverless: Databricks manages the server runtime.'

exercises.q: Who decides Photon?
exercises.explain: On classic CPU compute Photon is a toggle; on serverless it is enabled and managed; SQL warehouses also use Photon.

exercises.q: Which one is a compute *family* rather than an axis value?
exercises.explain: SQL Warehouse is a compute family. Photon (engine), DBR (runtime) and autoscaling (scaling) are axes/settings on a compute.

exercises.q: Explain why 'AWS VM m5.xlarge' and 'DBR 17.3 LTS' are not alternatives to each other.
exercises.model: They live on different axes: m5.xlarge is hardware (the machine), DBR 17.3 LTS is the software stack installed on it (Spark + Databricks software/libraries). A classic compute needs both: a VM type and a runtime.
rubric: Both are chosen together on classic
exercises.explain: Every classic config answers 'which machine?' and 'which software on it?' separately.

exercises.q: Which of these is NOT supported on serverless compute?
options: Instance pools and compute-scoped init scripts
exercises.explain: Serverless doesn't support compute policies, instance pools, compute-scoped init scripts, compute-scoped libraries or most Spark cluster configs — they're platform-managed. Photon and autoscaling are automatic on serverless Jobs.

exercises.q: A colleague wrote this **serverless Jobs** spec. Which lines are impossible?
exercises.fix:
Purpose: Jobs
Infrastructure: Serverless
Performance mode: Standard
exercises.explain: Worker type and min/max workers are infrastructure configuration that serverless manages for you. Performance mode (Standard vs Performance Optimized) IS a valid serverless Jobs setting.

exercises.q: Classic + Jobs + Standard + Multi-node + Autoscaling + Photon is a valid configuration.
exercises.explain: Completely sensible: a classic jobs compute with Standard access, several workers, autoscaling and Photon.

exercises.q: Example 1 (interactive ETL development) lists: Purpose, Infrastructure, Access mode, Runtime, Photon, Topology, Worker, Scaling, Driver. How many **computes** does it describe?
exercises.explain: One classic all-purpose compute with 9 configuration choices — not 9 or 10 computes.

exercises.q: Order the decision process for a classic compute.
items: Decide workload purpose (interactive / job / pipeline / SQL)
Land on the product (e.g. Classic Jobs)
Then set parameters: access mode, nodes, DBR, worker/driver type, scaling, Photon, spot, pools, termination
exercises.explain: Parameters come LAST. Only after you've chosen 'classic all-purpose' or 'classic Jobs' do Standard/Dedicated, DBR, workers etc. become relevant.

exercises.q: Match the classic matrix axis to its options.
exercises.explain: These are classic all-purpose/jobs configuration settings — the ones serverless removes.

exercises.q: Write the axis-by-axis spec (one `Axis: value` per line) for a **production scheduled ETL on classic jobs compute**: Standard access, DBR 17.3 LTS, Photon on, multi-node, autoscaling 4 → 20 workers.
exercises.solution:
Purpose: Jobs
Infrastructure: Classic
Access: Standard
Runtime: DBR 17.3 LTS
Photon: ON
Topology: Multi-node
Autoscaling: 4 -> 20 workers
exercises.explain: This is exactly the source's example 2 — one Classic Jobs Compute with specific parameters. LTS suits production; autoscaling bounds are yours on classic.

exercises.q: Now write the **serverless equivalent** of that ETL spec (only the lines you still choose; one `Axis: value` per line).
exercises.explain: Driver VM, worker VM, 2–20 workers, DBR 17.3, spot and pool all disappear. Autoscaling and Photon are enabled automatically on serverless Jobs.

exercises.q: Which serverless workload does NOT offer **Standard performance mode**?
exercises.explain: Standard performance mode exists for serverless Jobs and pipelines; notebooks use a performance-oriented interactive mode.

exercises.q: Standard access mode and Standard performance mode are the same setting seen from two screens.
exercises.explain: No relation besides the English word. Standard **access** = security/isolation on classic compute. Standard **performance** = serverless cost vs startup trade-off.

exercises.q: Which 'Standard' is this about?

items.text: Who may use this classic compute?

exercises.explain: Same word, two unrelated concepts — a classic source of confusion and a likely exam trap.

exercises.q: Match each serverless performance mode to its trait.
exercises.explain: For nightly batch with no start-time SLA, Standard performance mode saves money.

exercises.q: Your serverless nightly job is cheap but finance's dashboard SLA was just moved earlier, and the job now starts too slowly to finish in time.

steps.prompt: What setting do you look at first?

options.text: The serverless performance mode (Standard vs Performance Optimized)
options.fb: Right — Standard mode trades slower startup for lower cost.

options.text: The access mode (Standard vs Dedicated)
options.fb: Access mode is security/isolation, and serverless doesn't expose it.

options.text: The worker type
options.fb: Serverless doesn't let you pick worker types.

steps.prompt: What change fits the new SLA?

options.text: Switch the job to Performance Optimized
options.fb: Faster startup, more latency-sensitive — at higher cost.

options.text: Move the job to a notebook on Standard performance
options.fb: Notebooks don't even have Standard performance mode.

options.text: Add an instance pool
options.fb: Pools aren't supported on serverless.

exercises.explain: Performance mode is THE serverless knob for start-up latency vs cost. Don't confuse it with Standard access mode.

exercises.q: Which SQL warehouse type has Photon + Predictive IO but NOT Intelligent Workload Management?
exercises.explain: Classic = Photon; Pro = Photon + Predictive IO; Serverless = Photon + Predictive IO + Intelligent Workload Management.

exercises.q: A notebook attached only to a SQL warehouse can run `from pyspark.sql import functions as F`.
exercises.explain: A notebook on a SQL warehouse can run SQL and Markdown cells only — not Python/R. Use serverless notebook compute or all-purpose for PySpark.

exercises.q: Match the SQL warehouse matrix row to its correct 'Classic' column value.
exercises.explain: Classic warehouses have Photon but neither Predictive IO nor IWM, keep custom networking flexibility, and are the fallback/basic option. Serverless is the recommended default.

exercises.q: Notebook attached to `analytics-wh` (a SQL warehouse). Which cell will fail?
lines: from pyspark.sql import functions as F
SELECT country, SUM(amount) FROM prod.sales.orders GROUP BY country;
exercises.fix: Remove the Python cell, or attach the notebook to serverless notebook compute / all-purpose compute to run PySpark.
exercises.explain: SQL warehouses only execute SQL and Markdown in notebooks. The Python cell fails; the Markdown and SQL cells work.

exercises.q: Write a query you CAN run in a notebook attached to a SQL warehouse: total `amount` per `country` from `prod.sales.orders`.
exercises.explain: SQL cells run on a SQL warehouse; the same logic in PySpark (`groupBy(...).sum(...)`) would need Spark compute.

exercises.q: Order the warehouse types from FEWEST to MOST features (Photon / Predictive IO / IWM).
exercises.explain: Each step up adds one: Predictive IO at Pro, Intelligent Workload Management at Serverless.

exercises.q: All current SQL warehouse types support Photon.
exercises.explain: Serverless, Pro and Classic all have Photon; they differ in Predictive IO and Intelligent Workload Management.

exercises.q: 100 analysts run SQL from **Power BI**. What do you start with?
exercises.explain: SQL/BI workload → SQL warehouse → usually Serverless SQL Warehouse, recommended today for BI, SQL ETL and exploratory analytics.

exercises.q: You want to develop in **R** interactively. Which compute?
exercises.explain: Serverless notebooks don't support R. Interactive + unsupported serverless feature → classic all-purpose, possibly Dedicated depending on the workload.

exercises.q: Interactive PySpark exploration of 500 GB, no special requirements?
exercises.explain: Step 1: interactive. Step 2: no custom infra → serverless notebook compute. No worker VMs to decide.

exercises.q: Nightly ETL uses a **custom Spark JAR and low-level Spark functionality** that serverless doesn't support. Which compute?
exercises.explain: Automated + classic required → Classic Jobs Compute, then choose DBR, workers, autoscaling, access mode, Photon. Without that constraint, serverless Jobs would be the default.

exercises.q: Match the task to its best default compute (usage matrix).
exercises.explain: The usage matrix mirrors Databricks' task-support matrix: serverless defaults everywhere except where a classic-only feature (spark-submit) is needed; SQL-shaped tasks go to warehouses.

exercises.q: Order the questions in the decision diagram.
items: What is my workload? (interactive / job / pipeline / SQL)
Do I need custom infra or an unsupported serverless feature?
Pick the product (e.g. serverless notebook vs classic all-purpose)
If classic: configure Standard/Dedicated, Single/Multi, Fixed/Autoscale, CPU/GPU, DBR, Photon
exercises.explain: Workload first, infrastructure second, parameters last. Once this is clear, Compute → Create compute stops looking like dozens of unrelated checkboxes.

exercises.q: Serverless or classic required?

items.text: Nightly 2 a.m. ETL in Python, nothing special
Custom JAR with low-level Spark features
Exploring a 500 GB table in PySpark

exercises.explain: Default to serverless; fall back to classic only for unsupported features (R, RDD APIs, spark-submit, custom low-level JARs…).

exercises.q: A teammate says: "I need interactive compute, so I'll create a serverless all-purpose cluster with Dedicated access, 2–8 workers and DBR 17.3."

steps.prompt: What's wrong in the first part?

options.text: There is no 'serverless all-purpose cluster' — interactive + serverless is serverless notebook compute
options.fb: Correct — interactive + classic is all-purpose; interactive + serverless is a differently named product.

options.text: Nothing — that product exists
options.fb: It doesn't exist under that name; the matrix is constrained.

options.text: All-purpose can't be interactive
options.fb: All-purpose is interactive by design.

steps.prompt: If they really need Dedicated, 2–8 workers and DBR 17.3, what do they need?

options.text: Classic all-purpose compute
options.fb: Those are all classic infrastructure knobs.

options.text: Serverless notebook with a Dedicated toggle
options.fb: Serverless has no access-mode, worker or DBR selector.

options.text: Serverless SQL warehouse
options.fb: Warehouses don't have Standard/Dedicated or DBR selectors either.

exercises.explain: Purpose and infrastructure are different axes, but the matrix is constrained: classic exposes the knobs; serverless hides them.

exercises.q: In the 'all combinations' matrix, Classic Jobs lets you configure access mode, nodes, DBR and autoscaling, while Serverless Jobs exposes none of them.
exercises.explain: Classic Jobs: ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅. Serverless Jobs: ❌ access, ❌ nodes, ❌ traditional DBR, ❌ autoscaling (infra managed).

exercises.q: In the 'all combinations' matrix, how are DBR and autoscaling described for **Pro/Classic SQL warehouses**?
options: You pick a DBR; min/max workers
exercises.explain: Non-serverless warehouses use the Databricks SQL runtime (no DBR selector) and scale as warehouses (warehouse autoscale), with access via the warehouse model. Nodes are abstracted.

exercises.q: Interview question: "Walk me through how you would choose compute for a new workload in Databricks."
exercises.model: First I identify the workload: interactive development, an automated job, a Lakeflow pipeline or SQL/BI. SQL/BI goes to a SQL warehouse, usually serverless. For the others I ask whether I need anything serverless doesn't support (R, RDD APIs, custom JAR/low-level Spark, init scripts, pools, specific Spark configs). If not, I pick serverless notebook / serverless Jobs / serverless pipeline. If I do, I choose the classic equivalent (all-purpose, Jobs compute, classic pipeline) and only then configure access mode, nodes, DBR, worker/driver types, scaling, Photon, spot, pools and termination.
exercises.explain: This is the decision diagram in prose: workload → infrastructure → parameters.

exercises.q: Complete the quiz answers.
exercises.text: Interactive PySpark without special needs → [[serverless notebook compute|serverless notebook]]. Scheduled PySpark production ETL → [[serverless jobs]] if supported, otherwise [[classic jobs|classic jobs compute]]. Power BI → usually [[serverless sql warehouse]].
exercises.explain: These four answers cover most real-life compute choices.

exercises.q: Complete the access-mode definitions.
exercises.text: Access mode is an axis mainly for classic [[all-purpose]] and [[jobs]] compute. [[Standard]]: many users share the compute with workload isolation. [[Dedicated]]: assigned to one user or group.
exercises.explain: Standard/Dedicated is the classic access-mode axis; serverless and SQL warehouses don't expose it.

exercises.q: A task that ran fine on a classic **Dedicated** cluster fails after you move it to **serverless Jobs**.

steps.prompt: What do you ask yourself first?

options.text: Does serverless Jobs use Standard access semantics that my code isn't compatible with?
options.fb: Yes — serverless Jobs requires Standard-compatible workloads.

options.text: Did serverless forget to enable Photon?
options.fb: Photon is automatic on serverless Jobs and wouldn't break compatibility.

options.text: Is the serverless worker type too small?
options.fb: You can't choose worker types on serverless; that isn't the lever.

steps.prompt: The code relies on a Dedicated-only feature and can't be refactored now. What do you do?

options.text: Run it on classic Jobs compute with Dedicated access
options.fb: Only classic exposes Dedicated access mode.

options.text: Set Access mode = Dedicated in the serverless job
options.fb: Serverless has no such dropdown.

options.text: Run it on a SQL warehouse
options.fb: Warehouses have no Dedicated mode and don't run arbitrary Spark code.

exercises.explain: Serverless Jobs = Standard access semantics. Dedicated-only workloads stay on classic.

exercises.q: Order the debug steps for an unpredictable production job.
items: Check which compute the job runs on
Check who else is attached to that cluster during the run
Move the job to serverless Jobs or classic Jobs compute
exercises.explain: Compute first, then contention evidence, then move to the intended operational compute.

exercises.q: You migrate a classic job to serverless Jobs and can't find where to set the instance pool, the init script and `min_workers`.

steps.prompt: What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: Serverless doesn't support pools, compute-scoped init scripts or worker counts — they're platform-managed
options.fb: Exactly; the infrastructure matrix disappears on serverless.

options.text: You lack CAN MANAGE on the job
options.fb: Permissions don't hide these fields; they simply don't exist on serverless.

options.text: The fields are under Advanced → Spark config
options.fb: Most Spark cluster configs are also not supported on serverless.

steps.prompt: The init script installs a native library the job truly needs. Next step?

options.text: Run this task on Classic Jobs compute
options.fb: Classic exposes init scripts, pools and worker settings.

options.text: Add the init script to the serverless notebook instead
options.fb: Compute-scoped init scripts aren't supported on serverless anywhere.

options.text: Use a bigger serverless performance mode
options.fb: Performance mode affects startup/cost, not native installs.

exercises.explain: Serverless removes policies, pools, compute-scoped init scripts/libraries and most Spark configs. Truly required → classic.

exercises.q: Order the 'missing field on serverless' playbook.
items: Am I on serverless or classic?
Is the setting an infrastructure concern (VMs, counts, pools, init scripts, policies)?
Do I truly need it or is it a classic habit?
If truly needed, switch the task to Classic Jobs compute
exercises.explain: Identify the compute, classify the setting, challenge the need, then switch only if required.

exercises.q: In a notebook, `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM prod.sales.orders` works but the next cell `from pyspark.sql import functions as F` errors.

options.text: What compute the notebook is attached to
options.fb: If it's a SQL warehouse, only SQL and Markdown run.

options.text: Whether `prod.sales.orders` exists
options.fb: The SQL cell already worked; the table is fine.

options.text: Whether Photon is enabled
options.fb: Photon doesn't control which languages run.

options.text: Attach to serverless notebook compute (or all-purpose) for the Python cells
options.fb: Python/PySpark needs Spark compute.

options.text: Upgrade the warehouse from Pro to Serverless
options.fb: No warehouse type runs Python notebook cells.

options.text: Grant CAN MANAGE on the warehouse
options.fb: It's not a permission problem.

exercises.explain: Notebooks on SQL warehouses run SQL + Markdown only.

exercises.q: Order the questions for a serverless job with a startup-latency problem.
items: Is it a serverless Job/pipeline (not a notebook)?
Does the workload need fast startup or is it relaxed batch?
Switch to Performance Optimized (or Standard for cheaper batch)
exercises.explain: Identify, read the mode, match it to the SLA, then switch.

exercises.q: A data scientist's R notebook won't run on serverless notebook compute.

options.text: Does serverless notebook compute support R?
options.fb: It doesn't — R (and RDD APIs) are unsupported on serverless notebooks.

options.text: Is the cluster's DBR too old?
options.fb: Serverless has no user-chosen DBR.

options.text: Is the SQL warehouse stopped?
options.fb: Not relevant to a serverless notebook.

steps.prompt: Best compute for this R development?

options.text: Classic all-purpose, possibly Dedicated
options.fb: Interactive + unsupported serverless feature → classic all-purpose.

options.text: Serverless Jobs
options.fb: Still serverless, and not interactive.

options.text: Pro SQL warehouse
options.fb: Warehouses run SQL only.

exercises.explain: Interactive + unsupported serverless feature → classic all-purpose (maybe Dedicated).

exercises.q: You configure a classic all-purpose cluster with GPU instances and DBR ML and notice the Photon toggle can't be turned on.

options.text: Photon isn't supported on GPU instance types
options.fb: Axis constraint: GPU + Photon ❌ on classic.

options.text: You need Dedicated access for Photon
options.fb: Photon has nothing to do with access mode.

options.text: DBR ML is too old
options.fb: It's the GPU instance type, not the runtime version.

steps.prompt: The team also runs heavy SQL ETL in the same notebook. Best approach?

options.text: Run the SQL/ETL on a CPU compute with Photon; keep GPU compute for deep learning
options.fb: Different axes, different needs.

options.text: Force Photon via Spark config
options.fb: Not supported — don't fight the constraint.

options.text: Switch to single-node
options.fb: Topology doesn't unlock Photon on GPU.

exercises.explain: Not all axis combinations are valid: GPU + Photon on classic GPU compute is the classic example.

exercises.q: Complete the list of things serverless does NOT support.
exercises.text: Serverless does not support compute [[policies]], instance [[pools]], compute-scoped [[init scripts]], compute-scoped [[libraries]] or most Spark cluster [[configurations|configs]].
exercises.explain: These are infrastructure-level concerns that the platform manages on serverless.
